common_name: Insignis Angel's Trumpet (Frilled White Angel's Trumpet)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after all frost danger in fertile, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Brugmansia insignis prefers more consistent humidity and shade than the sun-tolerant x candida hybrids. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.

directions: Brugmansia insignis is a lowland South American species distinguished from other angel's trumpets by its long, narrow, pendulous flowers whose corolla lobes are often reflexed and finely fringed at the tips, and by a papery calyx that splits and peels back only partway rather than fully enclosing the flower tube like B. suaveolens. Flowers open white to very pale pink and can develop a faint blush as they age, releasing the genus's characteristic heavy sweet fragrance most strongly after dark. It prefers more shade and steadier humidity than the more sun-tolerant hybrid angel's trumpets, wilting readily if allowed to dry out between waterings. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, containing the same tropane alkaloids found throughout the genus, so site it away from children and pets.

common_name: Volcano Angel's Trumpet (Andean Orange Angel's Trumpet)

planting.note: Root cuttings and grow on in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade; like B. sanguinea, this high-elevation Andean species prefers cool nights and struggles in humid Gulf Coast summer heat, so afternoon shade and good air movement help it perform. All parts are toxic if ingested.

directions: Native to cool, high-elevation volcanic slopes of Colombia and Ecuador, Brugmansia vulcanicola is a close relative of the red-flowered B. sanguinea but bears narrower, more tubular orange-red flowers covered in fine, velvety hairs, held in a more upright-to-horizontal position rather than fully pendulous. Like B. sanguinea it is adapted to cool mountain conditions and blooms best where nights stay mild, making it better suited to coastal or highland climates than to hot, humid Gulf Coast summers; give it afternoon shade and consistent moisture during warm spells. Hummingbirds are the natural pollinators of its narrow, nectar-rich flowers. As with all Brugmansia, every part of the plant is highly toxic if ingested and should be kept away from children and pets.

common_name: Ballerina Purple Datura (Triple-Layered Purple Devil's Trumpet)

planting.note: Start seed indoors about 6 weeks before last frost, or direct sow once soil is reliably above 70°F; nick the hard seed coat and soak overnight to speed erratic germination. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.

directions: WARNING: ALL PARTS OF THIS PLANT ARE HIGHLY TOXIC — handle with care and site away from children and pets. 'Ballerina Purple' is a triple-layered selection of Datura metel, its flowers built from three nested corollas one inside the next so each upward-facing, deep violet-purple trumpet reads as a ruffled, tutu-like rosette rather than the simple single or lightly doubled flower of the species. Blooms open in late afternoon and continue through the night, carrying the same heavy sweet fragrance typical of the species. Grow in full sun in average to lean, well-drained soil, since overly rich soil favors foliage over flowers, and expect the shrubby plant to bloom continuously from midsummer until frost.

planting.note: Start seed indoors about 6 weeks before last frost, or direct sow once soil is reliably above 70°F; nick the seed coat and soak overnight to improve germination. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.

directions: WARNING: ALL PARTS OF THIS PLANT ARE HIGHLY TOXIC — handle with care and site away from children and pets. This old heirloom selection, sometimes sold as 'horn of plenty,' bears fully double flowers formed of one trumpet nested inside another, dark purple on the outer surface and streaked with white toward the throat of the inner corolla, a two-layer form distinct from the frillier three-layer blooms of 'Ballerina Purple'. Like other Datura metel forms, it opens its upward-facing flowers in late afternoon and into the evening with a strong sweet fragrance, and grows quickly into a bushy, well-branched plant in a single season. Plant in full sun in lean to average, well-drained soil, which encourages heavier bloom than overly rich ground.

planting.note: Direct sow at or just after last frost once soil has warmed to at least 70°F; lightly scarify seeds to improve germination. All parts of the plant are highly toxic if ingested.

directions: WARNING: ALL PARTS OF THIS PLANT ARE HIGHLY TOXIC — leaves, flowers, seeds, and roots contain potent tropane alkaloids and can cause severe poisoning; site away from children and pets and wash hands after handling. Datura innoxia is easily told apart from D. wrightii by its densely velvety, soft gray-green leaves and stems, covered in fine down that gives the whole plant a felted texture, and by white flowers often flushed with pale lavender toward the flaring lobes rather than pure white. Native from Mexico into the southwestern United States and south into parts of South America, it was used ceremonially by a number of indigenous peoples for its powerful psychoactive effects. Flowers open at dusk and close by mid-morning, drawing large sphinx moths as pollinators. Direct sow into well-drained, sandy or loamy soil in full sun after the soil has warmed; the plant tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil once established and self-seeds readily in zones 8–11.

common_name: Big Momma Turk's Cap (Giant-Flowered Native Turk's Cap)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery plants in spring once frost danger has passed; this selection grows noticeably larger in leaf, flower, and overall stature than typical wild Turk's cap, so give it extra room to spread.

directions: 'Big Momma' is a robust selection of the native Texas Turk's cap prized for producing markedly larger leaves and larger, more substantial twisted red flowers than the typical wild form, while keeping the same twisted, never-fully-open bloom shape that gives the plant its name. It grows into a bigger, bulkier clump than straight drummondii or the pink 'Pam Puryear' selection, and its extra flower size makes it especially conspicuous to hummingbirds, which visit continuously from summer into fall. Grow in morning sun with afternoon shade or filtered light beneath trees, and water regularly through the first season while the woody base establishes. It dies back to the ground in hard winter freezes but returns reliably from the roots each spring, quickly regaining its large scale by midsummer.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring after frost danger passes; because the variegation is not stable from seed, 'Fiesta' is propagated only by cuttings. Site in partial shade to protect the pale leaf variegation from scorching in full summer sun.

directions: 'Fiesta' is a foliage-variegated sport of the native Turk's cap, its leaves irregularly marbled in cream and green rather than the solid deep green of the wild species, giving it ornamental value even between flushes of bloom. It still produces the same bright red, spirally twisted flowers that never fully open, and remains just as attractive to hummingbirds and butterflies as green-leaved Turk's caps. Because the variegated tissue carries less chlorophyll, it grows a bit more slowly and is somewhat more sensitive to intense afternoon sun and hard freezes than solid-green forms, so a site with morning sun and afternoon shade suits it best. Like other Turk's caps it dies back in hard winter freezes and resprouts from the root crown in spring, though full leaf variegation may take a few weeks to reappear on new growth.
